# Imaging Apparatus and Information Processing System for Efficient Video Data Transmission

## Overview

The present disclosure relates to an imaging apparatus and an information processing system that address a significant challenge in modern video transmission: the need to reduce the volume of video data transmitted over a network while simultaneously minimizing the power consumption of the imaging apparatus itself. As video resolution and frame rates continue to increase, the demands placed on both network bandwidth and device power budgets grow correspondingly, making it essential to develop solutions that can intelligently reduce data at the source without requiring computationally expensive processing that would otherwise increase power draw.

## Image Sensor Configuration

At the core of the imaging apparatus is an image sensor equipped with an imaging surface on which a large number of pixels are arranged in a systematic vertical and horizontal grid pattern. This grid-based arrangement forms the fundamental structure through which incoming light is captured and converted into electrical signals representing the captured scene. The regular, two-dimensional layout of pixels enables structured and predictable access to image data, which is essential for the selective processing techniques described below.

## Pixel Control Unit and Block-Based Sampling

To manage the image sensor efficiently, the imaging apparatus incorporates a pixel control unit responsible for partitioning the imaging surface into a plurality of discrete blocks. Rather than processing the entire imaging surface uniformly, the pixel control unit applies a sampling function independently to each block. This block-based approach allows for localized control over how image data is captured and processed, providing flexibility that can be tailored to the characteristics of each region of the image.

Within each individual block, the pixel control unit performs a selective sampling operation: it identifies and selects specific pixels that correspond to the sampling function assigned to that block. Rather than reading out and transmitting the values of every pixel within the block, the pixel control unit outputs a sampling signal that is derived exclusively from the pixel values of the selected pixels. This selective readout mechanism is central to the data and power reduction achieved by the apparatus, as it inherently limits the amount of pixel data that needs to be processed and transmitted from the image sensor at the hardware level, rather than relying on downstream compression algorithms that would otherwise consume additional processing power.

## Reduced Image Generation

Complementing the pixel control unit, the imaging apparatus further includes a reduced image generating unit. This unit receives the sampling signals output from the image sensor for each of the partitioned blocks and uses them to construct a reduced image. By assembling the reduced image from the sampling signals—rather than from the full complement of pixel values captured across the imaging surface—the reduced image generating unit produces an image representation that is substantially smaller in data volume than a full-resolution image, while still preserving meaningful visual information derived from each block of the original scene.

## Summary

Through the coordinated operation of the block-partitioning pixel control unit and the reduced image generating unit, the disclosed imaging apparatus achieves a meaningful reduction in the amount of video data that must be transmitted over a network. Because the data reduction is accomplished through selective pixel sampling at the image sensor level, the apparatus avoids the additional power consumption typically associated with more computationally intensive image compression or processing techniques, thereby fulfilling the dual objectives of reduced network data volume and suppressed device power consumption.

# Technical Disclosure: Block-Based Image Sensor Sampling for Reduced Data Transmission

## Background

In modern network-connected imaging systems, such as security cameras, IoT devices, and remote monitoring equipment, two competing challenges must be balanced: the need to minimize data volume transmitted over networks and the need to reduce power consumption at the imaging apparatus itself. Traditional approaches to solving these problems often address only one issue at the expense of the other. For instance, software-based image compression techniques can reduce transmitted data volume but typically require significant processing power, which increases overall energy consumption. Conversely, simply reducing sensor resolution to save power results in a permanent loss of image quality and flexibility.

## Overview of the Disclosed Solution

The present disclosure addresses these interrelated challenges through a novel image sensor architecture that performs data reduction at the hardware level, before the image data is fully processed or transmitted. Rather than capturing a complete, full-resolution image and subsequently compressing it through computationally expensive software algorithms, the disclosed image sensor intelligently reduces the data volume during the initial sampling process itself.

## Detailed Description of the Block-Based Sampling Architecture

### Imaging Surface Partitioning

The core of the disclosed technology lies in a specialized image sensor whose imaging surface is divided into a plurality of discrete blocks. Each block encompasses a defined group of pixels, and the collection of blocks together spans the full imaging surface of the sensor. This partitioning may be implemented in various configurations depending on the desired resolution reduction ratio, image application requirements, and the physical characteristics of the sensor.

### Sampling Function Application

For each block within the partitioned imaging surface, the image sensor applies a sampling function designed to select one or more representative pixels from within that block. This sampling function may be implemented in several ways:

1. **Fixed-position sampling**: A predetermined pixel location within each block (e.g., the top-left pixel or the center pixel) is consistently selected as the representative pixel for that block.

2. **Value-based sampling**: The sampling function may select a pixel based on its value relative to other pixels in the block, such as choosing the pixel with the median brightness value, the highest signal-to-noise ratio, or another statistically significant characteristic.

3. **Adaptive sampling**: The sampling function may dynamically adjust which pixel is selected based on scene content, motion detection, or other contextual factors, allowing the sensor to prioritize regions of interest.

Regardless of the specific sampling strategy employed, the fundamental principle remains consistent: rather than processing and transmitting the full pixel data for every pixel within a block, only the value from the selected representative pixel is retained and utilized for subsequent processing.

### Generation and Output of Sampling Signals

Once the representative pixel has been selected for each block through application of the sampling function, the image sensor generates a sampling signal corresponding to that selected pixel's value. These sampling signals are then output from the image sensor as a collective dataset representing the entire imaging surface, but at a substantially reduced data volume compared to the raw, full-resolution pixel data.

This architecture is particularly advantageous because the data reduction occurs at the sensor level itself, meaning that the computationally intensive process of reading out and processing every individual pixel across the entire imaging surface is avoided. This directly translates into lower power consumption for the imaging apparatus, since fewer read operations and less data processing are required at the hardware level.

## Reduced Image Generation

The sampling signals output by the image sensor are subsequently provided to a reduced image generating unit, which is configured to construct a compact, reduced-resolution image based on these sampling signals. This reduced image generating unit performs the following functions:

1. **Signal reception**: The unit receives the stream of sampling signals corresponding to the representative pixels selected from each block across the imaging surface.

2. **Image reconstruction**: Using the received sampling signals, the reduced image generating unit assembles a coherent, compact image in which each pixel of the reduced image corresponds to one of the sampled blocks from the original imaging surface.

3. **Output for transmission**: The resulting reduced image, having a substantially smaller data volume than the original full-resolution image that would have been captured using conventional methods, is then made available for transmission over a network or for further processing.

## Advantages of the Disclosed Approach

The block-based sampling approach described herein offers several significant advantages over conventional imaging and data reduction techniques:

**Reduced Data Volume for Network Transmission**: By generating a compact image directly from selectively sampled pixel values, the volume of data that must be transmitted over a network is significantly decreased. This is particularly beneficial in bandwidth-constrained environments or in applications involving numerous simultaneously operating imaging devices, such as large-scale surveillance networks or distributed IoT sensor arrays.

**Lower Power Consumption**: Because the sampling and data reduction occur at the image sensor level—prior to full pixel readout and processing—the overall power requirements of the imaging apparatus are substantially reduced. This is especially advantageous for battery-powered or energy-constrained imaging devices, where extending operational lifespan is a critical design consideration.

**Scalability and Flexibility**: The block-based sampling architecture can be adapted to varying levels of data reduction by adjusting the size and configuration of the blocks, as well as the specific sampling function employed. This allows the disclosed system to be tailored to different application requirements, balancing image quality against data volume and power consumption as needed.

**Simplified Hardware Implementation**: Because the sampling function can be implemented directly within the image sensor's readout circuitry, the disclosed approach avoids the need for additional, power-hungry image processing hardware or software-based compression algorithms that would otherwise be required to achieve comparable data reduction after full-resolution image capture.

## Conclusion

By integrating block-based partitioning of the imaging surface with an intelligent sampling function at the sensor level, the disclosed technology provides an effective solution to the dual challenges of reducing network-transmitted data volume and minimizing power consumption in imaging apparatuses. The resulting reduced image generating unit leverages these efficiently sampled signals to construct compact images suitable for a wide range of applications, including remote monitoring, surveillance, and other network-connected imaging use cases where both bandwidth efficiency and power conservation are paramount design considerations.

# The Word "The"

"The" is the most commonly used word in the English language. As a definite article, it serves a simple yet essential grammatical function: pointing to something specific rather than something general.

## Grammatical Function

Unlike its counterpart "a" or "an" (the indefinite articles), "the" indicates that the speaker and listener both understand which particular object, person, or concept is being referenced. For example:

- "I saw a dog" suggests any dog, unspecified.
- "I saw the dog" implies a specific dog already known to both parties, perhaps mentioned earlier or obvious from context.

## Historical Origins

The word traces its roots back to Old English, derived from demonstrative pronouns like "se," "seo," and "þæt," which meant "that" or "this." Over centuries, these forms evolved and simplified into the single word "the" used today across all genders and numbers, unlike many other languages that maintain gendered articles (such as "le" and "la" in French).

## Usage Complexity

Despite its brevity, "the" carries significant complexity in usage:

- **Omission**: Certain contexts require no article at all, such as with proper nouns ("Paris," not "the Paris") or general plural nouns ("Dogs are loyal").
- **Idiomatic use**: Some expressions use "the" in ways that don't follow strict logical rules, such as "the more, the merrier."
- **Cross-linguistic challenge**: Speakers of languages without articles (like Russian, Japanese, or Mandarin) often find mastering "the" one of the more challenging aspects of learning English.

## Frequency and Significance

Linguistic studies consistently rank "the" as the most frequently used word in English texts, appearing far more often than any other word. Its ubiquity makes it a foundational building block of the language, despite carrying no concrete meaning on its own—its power lies entirely in the specificity it lends to the words that follow it.

In essence, this tiny three-letter word plays an outsized role in shaping clarity and precision within English communication.

# ABSTRACT

An imaging apparatus and information processing system are provided that reduce the volume of transmitted video data while lowering power consumption of the imaging device. The imaging apparatus includes an image sensor configured to capture image data, a detection unit configured to detect a predetermined region or a change condition within the captured image data, and a control unit configured to selectively extract and encode a partial region of the captured image data based on the detection result, rather than processing and transmitting the entire captured frame. The control unit adjusts at least one of a frame rate, resolution, or bit rate applied to the extracted partial region independently of the remaining image region, thereby reducing the processing load associated with image encoding. A communication unit transmits the encoded partial image data to an external information processing apparatus, which is configured to receive the transmitted data, reconstruct or analyze the region of interest, and generate output information reflecting a monitored condition. By limiting high-resolution or high-frame-rate processing to a dynamically determined region of interest, rather than the entire captured image, the imaging apparatus achieves a reduction in the amount of image data generated and transmitted per unit time, and correspondingly reduces power consumed by image-processing and communication circuitry. The information processing system further includes a setting unit configured to update the predetermined region or detection parameters based on feedback from the external apparatus, enabling adaptive control of the imaging apparatus over time. This configuration is applicable to monitoring cameras, network cameras, and battery-driven imaging devices requiring extended operational duration under constrained transmission bandwidth.

counterfactuals.output:
# Technical Disclosure Summary

## Title
**Block-Based Adaptive Pixel Sampling System for Image Sensors with Reduced Data Output**

---

## Field of the Disclosure

This disclosure relates to image sensor architectures, and more particularly to systems and methods for partitioning an imaging surface into discrete blocks, applying configurable sampling functions on a per-block basis, and generating a reduced-resolution or reduced-data-rate image output from selectively sampled pixel signals.

---

## Background

Conventional image sensors typically read out every pixel in the imaging array at a fixed resolution and frame rate, regardless of the informational content within different regions of the scene. This uniform readout approach results in several drawbacks:

- **High data bandwidth**: Full-resolution readout consumes significant bus bandwidth and downstream processing resources, even when large portions of the scene are static, low-detail, or of low interest.
- **High power consumption**: Reading and converting every pixel via analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) increases power draw, which is particularly problematic in battery-powered or thermally constrained devices.
- **Inflexible resource allocation**: Regions of interest (e.g., moving objects, faces, high-contrast edges) receive the same sampling treatment as uninteresting background regions, wasting resolution where it is not needed and under-resolving where it is.
- **Fixed sampling patterns**: Existing subsampling or binning schemes (e.g., uniform pixel skipping, fixed binning ratios) apply a single, static sampling strategy across the entire sensor, without the ability to adapt sampling density independently per region.

There exists a need for an image sensor architecture that can independently control the sampling strategy for different regions of the imaging surface, enabling reduced data output while preserving flexibility to prioritize sampling density where needed.

---

## Summary of the Disclosure

This disclosure describes an image sensor architecture in which the imaging surface (pixel array) is logically or physically partitioned into a plurality of **blocks**, each comprising a subset of the sensor's pixels (e.g., an N×M tile of the array). Each block is associated with a **sampling function** — a configurable rule or pattern that determines which pixels within that block are read out, how their signals are combined, and at what effective resolution or rate the block contributes to the final image.

The sensor includes:

1. **A block partitioning unit** that divides the pixel array into blocks according to a configurable grid (fixed size, variable size, or content-dependent boundaries).
2. **A per-block sampling controller** that applies an independently selectable sampling function to each block. Sampling functions may include:
   - Uniform subsampling (e.g., 1-in-N pixel selection)
   - Spatial binning (averaging or summing groups of pixels)
   - Weighted sampling (non-uniform selection favoring pixel sub-regions with higher local contrast or motion)
   - Random or pseudo-random sampling patterns (e.g., for compressive sensing applications)
   - Full-resolution passthrough (no reduction) for designated high-priority blocks
3. **A pixel signal selection/multiplexing stage** that gathers the sampled pixel signals from each block according to its assigned function.
4. **A reduced image generation unit** that assembles the selected/sampled pixel signals from all blocks into a composite reduced image, with a data volume smaller than a full-resolution readout of the entire array.

The sampling function assigned to each block may be:
- **Statically configured** at manufacture or system initialization (e.g., fixed foveation pattern), or
- **Dynamically adapted** during operation based on scene analysis, region-of-interest detection, motion detection, previous frame statistics, or external control signals (e.g., from a companion vision processor or ISP).

---

## Detailed Description

### 1. Imaging Surface Partitioning

The pixel array is divided into a grid of blocks. Block size and shape may be:
- **Fixed and uniform** (e.g., 16×16 pixel tiles across the entire array), simplifying addressing and control logic.
- **Non-uniform**, with smaller blocks in regions expected to contain fine detail (e.g., center of frame) and larger blocks in peripheral regions — a foveated layout.
- **Dynamically re-partitioned** on a frame-by-frame basis based on feedback from an image analysis engine (e.g., object detection results shifting fine-grained blocks to track a moving subject).

Block boundaries may align with existing sensor readout circuitry boundaries (e.g., column/row groups sharing readout buses) to simplify implementation, or may be logically defined in the digital domain after full analog readout.

### 2. Per-Block Sampling Function Assignment

Each block is associated with a sampling function selected from a library of supported functions, which may include but are not limited to:

| Sampling Function | Description | Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| Full readout | All pixels in block sampled | High-priority/ROI blocks |
| N:1 decimation | Every Nth pixel sampled | Uniform data reduction |
| 2×2, 4×4 binning | Neighboring pixels summed/averaged | Noise reduction, low-light |
| Checkerboard/quincunx sampling | Alternating pixel pattern | Balanced spatial coverage |
| Weighted/adaptive sampling | Sampling density proportional to local gradient/contrast | Edge/detail preservation |
| Random/pseudo-random sampling | Stochastic pixel selection | Compressive sensing, anti-aliasing |
| Temporal sampling | Block sampled at reduced frame rate | Static background regions |

A per-block configuration register or lookup table stores the assigned sampling function index and any associated parameters (e.g., decimation factor, binning kernel size, random seed).

### 3. Sampling Control and Signal Generation

A block-level sampling controller reads the configuration for each block and generates the corresponding **row/column select signals**, **ADC trigger timing**, and **analog combination (binning) control signals** needed to realize the assigned sampling function. This may be implemented via:

- Programmable row/column address generators per block region
- Shared ADC resources multiplexed across blocks according to sampling schedule
- In-pixel or near-pixel analog summing circuits for binning functions
- A digital post-processing path (if sampling is performed after full digital readout) that selects/downsamples pixel data per block according to the assigned function

### 4. Reduced Image Assembly

The pixel signals selected or generated per block are aggregated by a reduced image generation unit into an output image frame. Because different blocks may have different effective resolutions (due to differing sampling functions), the assembly unit may:

- Output a **variable-resolution composite image** with metadata indicating the sampling function/resolution used per block (for downstream reconstruction or interpretation), or
- **Upsample/interpolate** lower-sampled blocks to a uniform output grid for compatibility with standard image pipelines, while preserving the bandwidth savings at the sensor-to-processor interface, or
- Output a **compressed/packed data stream** where each block's data size varies according to its sampling function, accompanied by a block-map header.

### 5. Adaptive Feedback Loop (Optional Enhancement)

An optional feedback path allows an external or on-chip processor to analyze a previously captured reduced image (or a full-resolution calibration frame) and issue updated per-block sampling function assignments for subsequent frames. This enables:

- Region-of-interest tracking (e.g., increasing sampling density on a detected face or moving object across frames)
- Power-adaptive operation (e.g., reducing sampling globally when battery is low, or in specific blocks with static content)
- Bandwidth-adaptive operation (e.g., reducing per-block sampling rate under constrained output bus bandwidth)

---

## Example Implementation

Consider a sensor array of 4096×3072 pixels partitioned into 256×256 = 65,536 blocks, each 16×16 pixels. A scene analysis engine identifies a central region of interest occupying blocks corresponding to a 1024×768 area. The controller assigns:
- **Full readout** to blocks within the ROI
- **4:1 binning** to blocks immediately surrounding the ROI
- **8:1 decimation** to peripheral background blocks

The resulting reduced image preserves full detail in the region of interest while reducing overall data volume by an estimated 60–75% compared to full-frame readout, with corresponding reductions in ADC operations and output bus bandwidth.

---

## Advantages

- **Reduced data bandwidth** at the sensor output interface without uniformly sacrificing resolution across the entire frame.
- **Lower power consumption** by reducing the number of active ADC conversions and pixel readouts per frame.
- **Flexible, content-adaptive resolution allocation**, supporting foveated imaging, ROI tracking, and power/bandwidth-constrained operation.
- **Compatibility with existing ISP pipelines** via optional upsampling/normalization of block outputs to a uniform grid.
- **Scalability** across different sensor sizes and block granularities, applicable to still image, video, and machine-vision sensor products.

---

## Potential Variations

- Implementation entirely in the analog domain (sampling function realized via pixel-level or column-level analog circuitry) versus digital domain (full readout followed by digital block-wise selection/downsampling).
- Use of machine-learning-based controllers to predict optimal per-block sampling functions based on scene content, application context (e.g., autonomous navigation vs. photography), or historical frame statistics.
- Application to non-visible-spectrum sensors (e.g., IR, ToF, event-based sensors) using the same block-partition-and-sample architecture.
- Multi-tier block hierarchies (blocks composed of sub-blocks) enabling nested/recursive sampling function assignment.

---

## Conclusion

The disclosed block-based adaptive sampling image sensor architecture provides a flexible mechanism for reducing image data volume and power consumption by independently configuring the sampling strategy applied to each region of the imaging surface, while preserving the ability to maintain high fidelity in regions of interest. This approach is broadly applicable to consumer imaging, machine vision, surveillance, and any application benefiting from adaptive, bandwidth-efficient image capture.

# Summary of Invention

The present invention relates to a camera system and method for generating reduced-bandwidth image data through block-based pixel sampling, enabling efficient image transmission, storage, and processing while preserving essential visual information from a captured scene.

In one aspect, the invention provides an imaging apparatus comprising an image sensor configured to capture a full-resolution image comprising a plurality of pixels, and a processing unit configured to partition the full-resolution image into a plurality of discrete pixel blocks, each block comprising a predetermined arrangement of pixels (e.g., N×N pixel groupings). The processing unit is further configured to sample each pixel block according to a defined sampling scheme to select or derive a representative pixel value for that block, thereby generating a reduced image having a lower effective resolution and correspondingly reduced data size relative to the full-resolution image.

In some embodiments, the sampling scheme comprises selecting a single pixel from a predetermined position within each block (e.g., a corner or center pixel) as representative of that block. In other embodiments, the sampling scheme comprises computing an aggregate value, such as an average, median, weighted mean, or other statistical measure, derived from some or all pixels within the block, thereby providing a representative value that accounts for multiple pixels within the sampled region.

The reduced image, being substantially smaller in data size than the original full-resolution image, may be transmitted over a communication channel having limited bandwidth, stored in a memory having limited capacity, or subjected to further processing operations with reduced computational overhead, while still conveying sufficient visual information for applications including, but not limited to, preview generation, motion detection, image indexing, thumbnail creation, or transmission over networks with variable or constrained bandwidth availability.

In further embodiments, the block size, shape, or sampling scheme may be dynamically adjustable based on one or more operating parameters, including available bandwidth, desired image quality, processing capability of a receiving device, battery status, or user-defined preferences. This allows the system to adaptively balance image fidelity against resource constraints in real time.

Additional embodiments provide for the reduced image to be transmitted or stored in conjunction with metadata identifying the block size, sampling scheme, or sampling positions used in generating the reduced image, such that a receiving device or downstream process may appropriately interpret, reconstruct, or further process the reduced image data.

In another aspect, the invention provides a method comprising the steps of capturing an image via an image sensor, dividing the captured image into a plurality of pixel blocks, sampling each pixel block to obtain a representative pixel value, and assembling the representative pixel values into a reduced image, wherein the reduced image comprises a data size that is smaller than the data size of the captured image by a factor corresponding to the block size utilized.

In yet another aspect, the invention provides a non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions that, when executed by one or more processors, cause the one or more processors to perform the block-based pixel sampling operations described herein.

The described embodiments provide advantages including reduced power consumption associated with data transmission, decreased memory and storage requirements, improved responsiveness in bandwidth-constrained environments, and enhanced compatibility with downstream systems having limited processing resources, all while retaining sufficient image content for a variety of practical applications. It will be appreciated that the foregoing summary is illustrative only and is not intended to limit the scope of the invention, which is defined by the claims appended hereto.

---

# Abstract

An image sensor system and method are disclosed for generating a reduced-resolution image through selective pixel sampling, thereby enabling faster readout and lower processing overhead compared to full-frame acquisition and subsequent downscaling.

The system comprises an image sensor having a plurality of pixels arranged in a two-dimensional array, a pixel control unit, and a reduced image generating unit. The pixel control unit divides the image sensor's surface into a plurality of blocks, each block containing a predetermined number of pixels arranged in rows and columns. For each block, the pixel control unit selects one or more sampling pixels according to a designated selection pattern, which may be fixed, periodically varied, or dynamically adjusted based on imaging conditions such as scene brightness, motion detection, or a specified reduction ratio. The selection pattern may be uniform across all blocks or may vary between blocks to preserve image detail in regions of interest while further reducing data in less critical regions. The pixel control unit generates and transmits control signals to activate readout circuitry corresponding only to the selected sampling pixels within each block, while non-selected pixels remain unread or are read out at a lower priority, thereby reducing the volume of pixel data transferred from the sensor.

The reduced image generating unit receives the pixel signals output from the sampling pixels selected across all blocks and constructs a reduced-resolution image frame therefrom. Each sampling pixel's signal value is assigned to a corresponding position within the reduced image, such that the reduced image comprises one pixel value per block, effectively achieving a resolution reduction proportional to the block size. The reduced image generating unit may further apply interpolation, averaging, or noise-reduction processing using signal values from multiple sampling pixels within a block, where more than one sampling pixel per block is selected, to improve the fidelity of the representative pixel value.

The resulting reduced image may be used for preview display, auto-focus or auto-exposure evaluation, motion detection, image compression pre-analysis, or transmission bandwidth reduction, while the full-resolution image data remains selectively accessible for subsequent high-resolution capture. This selective sampling architecture reduces power consumption, readout time, and data bus load relative to conventional methods that first read out a full-resolution frame and then digitally downsample it, making it particularly advantageous for high-speed continuous shooting, video preview modes, and low-power imaging applications.

# Technical Field

The present disclosure relates to an imaging apparatus, and more particularly to an imaging apparatus including a pixel control unit and a reduced image generator configured to reduce the volume of image data transmitted over a network and to reduce power consumption associated with image capture, processing, and transmission operations.

# Summary

In recent years, imaging apparatuses such as network cameras and monitoring cameras have become widely deployed in surveillance systems, industrial automation, and Internet of Things (IoT) environments. As the resolution of image sensors continues to increase, the volume of image data generated per frame and per unit time has grown substantially. Transmitting such high-resolution image data continuously over a network places significant demands on network bandwidth and increases the power consumption of both the imaging apparatus and the associated communication circuitry. In battery-powered or otherwise power-constrained imaging apparatuses, this increased power consumption is particularly problematic, as it shortens operational lifetime and necessitates more frequent battery replacement or recharging.

Conventional approaches to reducing data volume include compressing captured images prior to transmission or lowering the frame rate or resolution of the entire image uniformly. However, uniform reduction of resolution or frame rate often degrades image quality in regions of interest that may be important for a given application, such as regions containing moving objects or specific target subjects. Furthermore, conventional compression techniques still require the imaging apparatus to read out, process, and at least partially encode the full pixel array for every frame, which does not sufficiently reduce the power consumed by the pixel array driving circuitry and the analog-to-digital conversion circuitry.

Accordingly, there is a need for an imaging apparatus capable of selectively controlling which pixels or pixel regions of an image sensor are driven and read out, and of generating a reduced image based on the readout pixel data, so as to decrease both the amount of image data transmitted over a network and the power consumed during image capture and processing, while still providing image data of sufficient quality for its intended purpose.

To address the foregoing problems, an imaging apparatus according to an embodiment of the present disclosure includes an image sensor having a plurality of pixels arranged in a matrix, a pixel control unit, and a reduced image generator. The pixel control unit is configured to control driving of the pixels such that pixel signals are selectively read out from a subset of the plurality of pixels, rather than from all pixels of the image sensor, based on a predetermined condition such as a designated region of interest, a thinning-out pattern, or an operating mode of the imaging apparatus. The reduced image generator is configured to generate a reduced image, having a smaller data amount than an image obtained by reading out all of the pixels, using the pixel signals read out from the subset of pixels selected by the pixel control unit.

By selectively driving and reading out only a portion of the pixels of the image sensor, the imaging apparatus can reduce the power consumed by the pixel driving circuitry and the analog-to-digital conversion circuitry as compared to an apparatus that reads out the entire pixel array for every frame. In addition, because the reduced image generated by the reduced image generator has a smaller data amount than a full-resolution image, the amount of image data that must be transmitted over a network to an external apparatus, such as a server or a recording apparatus, is correspondingly reduced. This, in turn, reduces the power consumed by the communication circuitry of the imaging apparatus and lessens the burden placed on the network. Furthermore, because the pixel control unit can adaptively select which pixels are read out based on a predetermined condition, the imaging apparatus can maintain image quality in regions of particular interest while reducing the overall data amount and power consumption associated with regions of lesser importance.

According to further embodiments, the pixel control unit may vary the subset of pixels to be read out in accordance with a detected motion region, a user-designated region, or a change in operating state of the imaging apparatus, and the reduced image generator may generate the reduced image by any of interpolation, thinning-out, addition, or other pixel-signal combination processing applied to the readout pixel signals. These and other embodiments, together with their attendant advantages, will become apparent from the detailed description, the accompanying drawings, and the appended claims.
